overview:
Cardiomyopathy is a disease of the heart muscle that makes it harder for the heart to pump blood to the rest of the body and can lead to symptoms of heart failure. It can also lead to other serious heart conditions. There are various types, including dilated, hypertrophic, and restrictive cardiomyopathy. Treatment includes medicines and sometimes surgically implanted devices and heart surgery. Some people with severe cardiomyopathy need a heart transplant. Treatment depends on the type of cardiomyopathy and how serious it is.
+Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is one of the most common inherited cardiac disorders, with prevalence around 1 in 500 people and annual mortality around 1 to 2 percent. It is produced by mutations in multiple genes coding for sarcomeric proteins and is primarily autosomal dominant with variable penetrance. The chief abnormality is left ventricular hypertrophy occurring without an inciting stimulus such as hypertension or aortic stenosis. Dilated cardiomyopathy is characterized by ventricular dilatation and global myocardial dysfunction with ejection fraction less than 40 percent. Restrictive cardiomyopathy is the least common form and occurs in advanced stages of infiltrative disease such as haemochromatosis, amyloidosis, or sarcoidosis.
ecg_clues: left ventricular hypertrophy with increased precordial voltages and non-specific ST segment and T-wave abnormalities in HCM
deep narrow dagger-like Q waves in lateral leads I aVL V5-6 in HCM
deep narrow dagger-like Q waves in inferior leads II III aVF in HCM
left atrial enlargement in HCM
short PR and delta wave with WPW in some HCM cases
atrial fibrillation and supraventricular tachycardias in HCM
PACs PVCs VT in HCM
giant precordial T-wave inversions in apical HCM
left atrial enlargement in DCM
biatrial enlargement in DCM
left ventricular hypertrophy or biventricular enlargement in DCM
left bundle branch block in DCM
right bundle branch block in DCM
left axis deviation in DCM
poor R-wave progression with QS complexes in V1-4 in DCM
frequent ventricular ectopics and ventricular bigeminy in DCM
ventricular dysrhythmias VT or VF in DCM
reduced voltage QRS complexes in limb leads in DCM with diffuse fibrosis
abnormal Q waves V1 to V4 pseudoinfarction pattern in DCM
low voltage QRS complexes in restrictive cardiomyopathy
non-specific ST segment or T wave changes in restrictive cardiomyopathy
bundle branch blocks in restrictive cardiomyopathy
atrioventricular block in restrictive cardiomyopathy
pathological pseudo-infarction Q waves in restrictive cardiomyopathy
atrial and ventricular dysrhythmias in restrictive cardiomyopathy
ecg_limitations: no specific ECG features are unique to dilated cardiomyopathy
HCM Q waves can mimic prior myocardial infarction but have different morphology
a small subset of HCM patients have abnormal ECG without LVH on echo

common: shortness of breath or trouble breathing with activity or at rest
chest pain after physical activity or heavy meals
heartbeats that feel rapid pounding or fluttering
swelling of legs ankles feet stomach area and neck veins
bloating of the stomach area due to fluid buildup
red_flags: chest pain lasting more than a few minutes

causes: heart tissue damage from a heart attack
infections causing inflammation of the heart
metabolic disorders such as obesity thyroid disease or diabetes
lack of essential vitamins or minerals such as thiamin
massive anterior STEMI causing ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy
viral myocarditis such as coxsackie B or adenovirus
risk_factors: family history of cardiomyopathy heart failure or sudden cardiac arrest
illicit drug use such as cocaine amphetamines and anabolic steroids

history_questions: Do you have symptoms all the time or do they come and go?
What, if anything, seems to improve your symptoms?
What, if anything, appears to make your symptoms worse?
Do you have a family history of cardiomyopathy or heart disease?

goals: keep the condition from getting worse
medications: medicines to improve the heart's ability to pump blood
medicines to remove extra fluid and sodium
procedures: catheter ablation for irregular heart rhythm

prevention: avoid alcohol or illegal drugs such as cocaine
when_to_seek_help: chest pain lasting more than a few minutes

confidence_rules: exertional syncope or presyncope in HCM suggests LVOT obstruction or ventricular dysrhythmia
giant precordial T-wave inversion suggests apical HCM
deep narrow dagger-like Q waves in lateral leads support HCM
low voltage QRS complexes support restrictive cardiomyopathy in infiltrative disease
LBBB with signs of dilatation supports DCM
agent_reasoning_hints: HCM Q waves can mimic prior myocardial infarction but infarction Q waves are typically greater than 40 ms
HCM often shows LVH without hypertension or aortic stenosis
If HCM is suspected with syncope chest pain and characteristic ECG changes and echo is unremarkable, consider cardiac MRI
Dilated cardiomyopathy presents with biventricular failure and high mortality due to progressive cardiogenic shock or ventricular dysrhythmias
Restrictive cardiomyopathy may show conduction disturbances due to infiltrative disease
source_notes: HCM prevalence is around 1 in 500 with annual mortality around 1 to 2 percent
HCM is primarily autosomal dominant with variable penetrance
HCM is a leading cause of sudden cardiac death in young people
HCM commonly shows asymmetrical septal hypertrophy and may have LVOT obstruction
Apical HCM shows giant precordial T-wave inversion and a spade-shaped LV cavity
Dilated cardiomyopathy is characterized by ventricular dilatation and ejection fraction less than 40 percent
Dilated cardiomyopathy has high mortality with 2-year survival around 50 percent
Restrictive cardiomyopathy occurs in infiltrative disease such as haemochromatosis amyloidosis or sarcoidosis
Restrictive cardiomyopathy can show low voltage QRS complexes and conduction disturbances
In DCM, abnormal Q waves in V1 to V4 can mimic myocardial infarction
